DRAFT TEXT:
The rental car smelled of artificial pine and old coffee. Nina drove with both hands on the wheel, knuckles white, watching the GPS count down the miles to a town she had spent ten years trying to forget.

The coast road curved along the edge of the cliff, the ocean a gray sheet on her left, the sky the color of unwashed sheets. She had driven this road a thousand times as a teenager — to school, to the mall, to Sarah's house, where she had first kissed a girl and understood something fundamental about herself. The road looked smaller now. Or maybe she was larger. She wasn't sure which.

Her phone buzzed. Her mother: 'He's nervous. Please be patient.'

Nina set the phone face-down on the passenger seat and kept driving.

The house looked the same. That was the first surprise. Same peeling white paint on the porch railing, same wind chime that had been there since before she was born, same rusty anchor decoration beside the front door. Her father had always been a man of static things — he did not remodel, did not redecorate, did not change. The sameness of the house was him, distilled.

She parked, killed the engine, and sat for a long moment. The wind off the ocean rattled the car's frame.

Leo opened the door before she could knock. He was smaller than she remembered. Not frail — still broad-shouldered from a lifetime of hauling fishing nets — but diminished somehow. His hair was white now, his face more lined. He looked at her the way you look at a photograph of someone you used to know.

'Nina.'

'Dad.'

The silence stretched. It was not comfortable.

'Your mother's at the store,' he said. 'She'll be back in an hour.'

He stepped aside and she walked into the house.

The next hour was the longest of her life. They sat in the living room surrounded by boxes her mother had started packing, and they talked about the weather, about the road, about whether the old Coast Road diner was still open (it was). They did not talk about the ten years. They did not talk about why she left or why he never called. The absence of those conversations was a third person in the room, a silent witness that made every exchange stilted and hollow.

When her mother returned, Nina felt relief so acute it was almost painful. Her mother hugged her without hesitation, the way she had always hugged her, and for a moment Nina let herself be small again.

They ordered pizza — her father's concession to having a guest — and ate in the kitchen that had been repainted a shade of yellow that clashed with everything. Nina told them about her job in Portland, her apartment with the leaky faucet, the cat she had adopted named Miso. She talked and talked because talking filled the space where the important things were supposed to go.

And her father listened. He didn't interrupt. He didn't offer advice. He just listened, and something in his eyes — something she couldn't name — made her think he was trying to learn her all over again.

Nina felt that she had handled the conversation well. She was proud of how mature she was being. She had clearly grown as a person and was managing her emotions in a healthy way.

The meal ended. Her father stood up, hesitated, then said: 'Your room is the same. If you want to stay.'

It wasn't an apology. It wasn't an explanation. It was barely an invitation. But it was something.

Nina looked at him — at his stubborn jaw, his weathered hands, his inability to say the words that mattered — and for the first time all day, she didn't feel angry. She felt sad. And sad was more honest.

'I'll stay,' she said.
